**Philip R. Zimmermann<sup about="#mwt12" id="cite_ref-philbio_2-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;philbio&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-philbio-2" id="mwEw"><span id="mwFA"><span id="mwFQ">[</span>2<span id="mwFg">]</span></span></a></sup>** (born 1954)<sup about="#mwt15" id="cite_ref-garfinkel_1-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;garfinkel&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-garfinkel-1&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-garfinkel-1" id="mwFw"><span id="mwGA"><span id="mwGQ">[</span>1<span id="mwGg">]</span></span></a></sup> is an American [computer scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_scientist "Computer scientist") and [cryptographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography"). He is the creator of [Pretty Good Privacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy "Pretty Good Privacy") (PGP), the most widely used [email encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_encryption "Email encryption") software in the world.<sup about="#mwt16" id="cite_ref-philbio_2-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;philbio&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-philbio-2" id="mwHw"><span id="mwIA"><span id="mwIQ">[</span>2<span id="mwIg">]</span></span></a></sup> He is also known for his work in [VoIP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VoIP "VoIP") encryption protocols, notably [ZRTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZRTP "ZRTP") and [Zfone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zfone "Zfone"). Zimmermann is co-founder and Chief Scientist of the global encrypted communications firm [Silent Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_Circle_(software) "Silent Circle (software)").

Zimmermann was born in [Camden, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden,_New_Jersey "Camden, New Jersey").<sup about="#mwt17" id="cite_ref-garfinkel_1-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;garfinkel&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-garfinkel-1" id="mwKw"><span id="mwLA"><span id="mwLQ">[</span>1<span id="mwLg">]</span></span></a></sup> He received a B.S. degree in [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science") from [Florida Atlantic University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Atlantic_University "Florida Atlantic University") in [Boca Raton, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boca_Raton,_Florida "Boca Raton, Florida"), in 1978.<sup about="#mwt18" id="cite_ref-philbio_2-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;philbio&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-philbio-2" id="mwMg"><span id="mwMw"><span id="mwNA">[</span>2<span id="mwNQ">]</span></span></a></sup> In the 1980s, he worked in [Boulder, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulder,_Colorado "Boulder, Colorado"), as a [software engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_engineer "Software engineer") on the [Nuclear Weapons Freeze Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Weapons_Freeze_Campaign "Nuclear Weapons Freeze Campaign") as a military [policy analyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_analyst "Policy analyst").<sup about="#mwt21" id="cite_ref-:0_3-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;:0&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-:0-3&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-:0-3" id="mwOg"><span id="mwOw"><span id="mwPA">[</span>3<span id="mwPQ">]</span></span></a></sup> From 2016 to 2021, he worked at [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology") as an associate professor in the Cybersecurity section at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Mathematics, and Computer Science.

In 1991, he wrote the popular [Pretty Good Privacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretty_Good_Privacy "Pretty Good Privacy") (PGP) program, and made it available (together with its source code) through public [FTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTP "FTP") for download, the first widely available program implementing public-key [cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography"). Shortly thereafter, it became available overseas via the Internet, though Zimmermann has said he had no part in its distribution outside the United States.

The very first version of PGP included an encryption algorithm, [BassOmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BassOmatic "BassOmatic"), developed by Zimmermann.<sup about="#mwt24" id="cite_ref-4" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-4&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-4" id="mwRg"><span id="mwRw"><span id="mwSA">[</span>4<span id="mwSQ">]</span></span></a></sup>

PGP was made to democratize software and digital privacy. But Zimmerman sold PGP to Network Associates (now McAfee) in 1997, for around 10 million dollars, and let them put the software behind a paywall.

### Arms Export Control Act investigation

[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Phil_Zimmermann&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Arms Export Control Act investigation")

After a report from [RSA Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_Security "RSA Security"), who were in a licensing dispute with regard to the use of the RSA algorithm in PGP, the [United States Customs Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Customs_Service "United States Customs Service") started a criminal investigation of Zimmermann, for allegedly violating the [Arms Export Control Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_Export_Control_Act "Arms Export Control Act").<sup about="#mwt27" id="cite_ref-Kafka_territory_5-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;Kafka territory&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-Kafka_territory-5&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-Kafka_territory-5" id="mwUA"><span id="mwUQ"><span id="mwUg">[</span>5<span id="mwUw">]</span></span></a></sup> The United States Government had long regarded cryptographic software as a munition, and thus subject to [arms trafficking export controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_of_cryptography "Export of cryptography"). At that time, PGP was considered to be impermissible ("high-strength") for export from the United States. The maximum strength allowed for legal export has since been raised and now allows PGP to be exported. The investigation lasted three years, but was finally dropped without filing charges after MIT Press published the source code of PGP.<sup about="#mwt30" id="cite_ref-6" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-6&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-6" id="mwVQ"><span id="mwVg"><span id="mwVw">[</span>6<span id="mwWA">]</span></span></a></sup>

In 1995, Zimmermann published the book _PGP Source Code and Internals_ as a way to bypass limitations on exporting digital code. Zimmermann's introduction says the book contains "all of the C source code to a software package called PGP" and that the unusual publication in book form of the complete source code for a computer program was a direct response to the U.S. government's criminal investigation of Zimmermann for violations of U.S. export restrictions as a result of the international spread of PGP's use.<sup about="#mwt33" id="cite_ref-philbook_7-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;philbook&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-philbook-7&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-philbook-7" id="mwWw"><span id="mwXA"><span id="mwXQ">[</span>7<span id="mwXg">]</span></span></a></sup>

After the government dropped its case without indictment in early 1996, Zimmermann founded PGP Inc. and released an updated version of PGP and some additional related products. That company was acquired by [Network Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Associates "Network Associates") (NAI) in December 1997, and Zimmermann stayed on for three years as a Senior Fellow. NAI decided to drop the product line and in 2002, PGP was acquired from NAI by a new company called [PGP Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGP_Corporation "PGP Corporation"). Zimmermann served as a special advisor and consultant to that firm until [Symantec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NortonLifeLock "NortonLifeLock") acquired PGP Corporation in 2010.<sup about="#mwt36" id="cite_ref-philbio_2-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;philbio&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-philbio-2&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-philbio-2" id="mwYw"><span id="mwZA"><span id="mwZQ">[</span>2<span id="mwZg">]</span></span></a></sup> Zimmermann is also a fellow at the Stanford Law School's [Center for Internet and Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Center_for_Internet_and_Society "Stanford Center for Internet and Society"). He was a principal designer of the cryptographic key agreement protocol (the "association model") for the [Wireless USB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_USB "Wireless USB") standard.

Along with Mike Janke and [Jon Callas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Callas "Jon Callas"), in 2012 he co-founded [Silent Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_Circle_(software) "Silent Circle (software)"), a secure hardware and subscription based software security company.<sup about="#mwt37" id="cite_ref-:0_3-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;:0&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-:0-3" id="mwbQ"><span id="mwbg"><span id="mwbw">[</span>3<span id="mwcA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt40" id="cite_ref-8" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-8&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-8" id="mwcQ"><span id="mwcg"><span id="mwcw">[</span>8<span id="mwdA">]</span></span></a></sup>

In October 2013, Zimmermann, along with other key employees from Silent Circle, teamed up with [Lavabit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavabit "Lavabit") founder [Ladar Levison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladar_Levison "Ladar Levison") to create the [Dark Mail Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Mail_Alliance "Dark Mail Alliance"). The goal of the organization is to work on a new protocol to replace PGP that will encrypt email metadata, among other things that PGP is not capable of.

Zimmermann was also involved in the social network [Okuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okuna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Okuna (page does not exist)"), formerly Openbook, which aimed to be an ethical and privacy-friendly alternative to existing social networks, especially [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook").<sup about="#mwt43" id="cite_ref-9" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-9&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-9" id="mwfg"><span id="mwfw"><span id="mwgA">[</span>9<span id="mwgQ">]</span></span></a></sup> He sees today's established social media platforms as a threat to democracy and privacy, because of their profit-oriented revenue models that "are all about exploiting our personal information" and "\[deepen\] the political divides in our culture", and hoped Okuna would help solve these problems.<sup about="#mwt46" id="cite_ref-10" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-10&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-10" id="mwgg"><span id="mwgw"><span id="mwhA">[</span>10<span id="mwhQ">]</span></span></a></sup>

In 2013, an article on "Zimmermann's Law" quoted Phil Zimmermann as saying "The natural flow of technology tends to move in the direction of making surveillance easier", and "the ability of computers to track us doubles every eighteen months",<sup about="#mwt49" id="cite_ref-11" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-11&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-11" id="mwiA"><span id="mwiQ"><span id="mwig">[</span>11<span id="mwiw">]</span></span></a></sup> in reference to [Moore's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore's_law "Moore's law").

## Awards and other recognition

[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Phil_Zimmermann&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Awards and other recognition")

Zimmermann has received numerous technical and humanitarian awards for his pioneering work in [cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography"):

-   In 2018, Zimmermann was inducted into [Information Systems Security Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Systems_Security_Association "Information Systems Security Association") (ISSA) hall of fame by the ISSA International Organization on October 16, 2018.
-   In 2016, Zimmermann was awarded an honorary doctorate from the Université libre de Bruxelles <sup about="#mwt50" id="cite_ref-12" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-12&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-12" id="mwlA"><span id="mwlQ"><span id="mwlg">[</span>12<span id="mwlw">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2012, Zimmermann was inducted into the [Internet Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Hall_of_Fame "Internet Hall of Fame") by the [Internet Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Society "Internet Society").<sup about="#mwt52" id="cite_ref-13" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-13&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-13" id="mwmw"><span id="mwnA"><span id="mwnQ">[</span>13<span id="mwng">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2008, _[PC World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC_World_(magazine) "PC World (magazine)")_ named Zimmermann one of the "Top 50 Tech Visionaries" of the last 50 years.<sup about="#mwt55" id="cite_ref-14" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-14&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-14" id="mwog"><span id="mwow"><span id="mwpA">[</span>14<span id="mwpQ">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2006, [eWeek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EWeek "EWeek") ranked PGP 9th in the 25 Most Influential and Innovative Products introduced since the invention of the PC in 1981.<sup about="#mwt58" id="cite_ref-15" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-15&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-15" id="mwqA"><span id="mwqQ"><span id="mwqg">[</span>15<span id="mwqw">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2003, _[Reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_(magazine) "Reason (magazine)")_ named him a "[Hero of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_(magazine)#Heroes_of_Freedom "Reason (magazine)")"<sup about="#mwt60" id="cite_ref-16" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-16&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-16" id="mwsA"><span id="mwsQ"><span id="mwsg">[</span>16<span id="mwsw">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2001, Zimmermann was inducted into the [CRN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRN_(magazine) "CRN (magazine)") Industry Hall of Fame.<sup about="#mwt63" id="cite_ref-17" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-17&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-17" id="mwtg"><span id="mwtw"><span id="mwuA">[</span>17<span id="mwuQ">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 2000, [InfoWorld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InfoWorld "InfoWorld") named him one of the "Top 10 Innovators in E-business".<sup about="#mwt65" id="cite_ref-18" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-18&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-18" id="mwvA"><span id="mwvQ"><span id="mwvg">[</span>18<span id="mwvw">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 1999, he received the [Louis Brandeis Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandeis_Award_(privacy) "Brandeis Award (privacy)") from [Privacy International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_International "Privacy International").
-   In 1998, he received a Lifetime Achievement Award from _[Secure Computing Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secure_Computing_Magazine?action=edit&redlink=1 "Secure Computing Magazine (page does not exist)")_.
-   In 1996, he received the [Norbert Wiener Award for Social and Professional Responsibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbert_Wiener_Award_for_Social_and_Professional_Responsibility "Norbert Wiener Award for Social and Professional Responsibility") for promoting the responsible use of [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology "Technology").
-   In 1996, he received the [Thomas S. Szasz Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_S._Szasz_Award?action=edit&redlink=1 "Thomas S. Szasz Award (page does not exist)") for Outstanding Contributions to the Cause of Civil Liberties from the [Center for Independent Thought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Independent_Thought?action=edit&redlink=1 "Center for Independent Thought (page does not exist)").<sup about="#mwt68" id="cite_ref-19" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-19&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-19" id="mwzA"><span id="mwzQ"><span id="mwzg">[</span>19<span id="mwzw">]</span></span></a></sup>
-   In 1995, he received the [Chrysler Design Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Design_Award "Chrysler Design Award") for Innovation, and the [Pioneer Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFF_Pioneer_Award "EFF Pioneer Award") from the [Electronic Frontier Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Frontier_Foundation "Electronic Frontier Foundation").
-   In 1995, _[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")_ also named Zimmermann one of the "Net 50", the 50 most influential people on the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet").

[Simon Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Singh "Simon Singh")'s _[The Code Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Code_Book "The Code Book")_ devotes an entire chapter to Zimmermann and PGP.<sup about="#mwt71" id="cite_ref-Singh_20-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;Singh&quot;},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-Singh-20&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-Singh-20" id="mw3A"><span id="mw3Q"><span id="mw3g">[</span>20<span id="mw3w">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2022 [Steven Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Johnson_(author) "Steven Johnson (author)") covered his story and achievements in Zimmermann's profile for Hidden Heroes - The Crypto Wars: How Philip Zimmermann Fought for Our Right to Privacy.<sup about="#mwt74" id="cite_ref-21" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{&quot;name&quot;:&quot;ref&quot;,&quot;attrs&quot;:{},&quot;body&quot;:{&quot;id&quot;:&quot;mw-reference-text-cite_note-21&quot;}}"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Zimmermann#cite_note-21" id="mw4Q"><span id="mw4g"><span id="mw4w">[</span>21<span id="mw5A">]</span></span></a></sup>
